Republic of the Philippines DEPARTMENT or THE INTERIOR AND LOCAL GOVERNMENT A. Francisco Qold Condominium II, EDSA cor. Mapagrnahal St., Diliman, Quezon City OFFICE OF SECRETARY OPINION NO. 16 S. 2(D5 15 February 2005 MAYOR JESSE B. CASTILLO Bacoor, Cavite Dear Mayor Castillo: This has reference to your letter, requesting for legal opinion on the following issues: (1) quorum; (2) time of submission of enacted ordinance to the Office of the Mayor; and (3) declaration of state of calamity by the sanggunian. As could be inferred from your letter, you particularly raised questions on the following issues: 2. 3. 4. 5. 6. What is the required number Of sanggunian members present in order to constitute a quorum? Is there a prescribed time within which the sanggunian shall submit an enacted ordinance to the Municipal Mayor for his approval? Are Members of the Sangguniang Bayan required to sign on the enacted ordinance? If so, what are the liabilities if they refuse to sign for varied reasons, one of which is their demand for something in exchange of signing an enacted ordinance? In declaring a state of calamity, what is the required number of sanggunian members to be present in order to constitute a quorum when one member of that sanggunian is on leave? If the province declares a calamity, is it still necessary for the Sangguniang Bayan to pass a resolution declaring also the municipality under a state of calamity? If there is .a national declaration of a state of calamity, is the municipal government still required to declare its own state of calamity? In reply to your first query, it bears stressing that your Sangguniang Bayan is composed of eight (8) regular members; the Liga ng mga Barangay President, the SK Federation President and the Vice Mayor as Presiding Officer. May it be noted that in our long line of opinions, we consistently opined that the number of the Vice Mayor as Presiding Officer should be included in determining the number of quorum. The inclusion of the number of the Vice Mayor in determining the number of quorum was further bolstered by the Decision of the Supreme Court in Gamboa u. Aguirre (310 SCRA 867, 20 July 1999), where the Supreme Court ruled that when the Vice Mayor becomes the Acting Mayor, he is not anymore allowed to continue to preside over the sanggunian session as he will be expected to perform full- time executive functions.

-2- Moreover, Section 446 (a) of the Local Government Code provides, thus: "SEC. 446. Composition.- (a) The sangguniang bayan, the legislative body of the municipality, shall be composed of the municipal vice mayor as the presiding officer, the regular sanggunian members, the president of the municipal chapter of the Ziga ng mga barangay, the president of the pambayang pederasyon ng mga sangguniang kabataan, and the sectoral representatives, as members. " The foregoing would clearly show that the Vice Mayor, as Presiding Officer, is a composite member of the sanggunian. Hence, the intriguing issue as to whether or not the number of the Presiding Officer is to be included in determining the quorum of the sanggunian has already been resolved with the advent of the new Local Govemment Code of 1991 (RA 7160). The dilemma as to whether or not the number of the Presiding Officer is to be included in determining the number of quorum of the sanggunian was brought about by the fact that under the old Local Government Code (Batas Pambansa Blg. 337), the Presiding Officer then of the sanggunian was the Mayor. Hence, from the foregoing disquisition, it becomes more clear now that the legislative intent and the judicial wisdom is to provide a complete separation of powers and functions between the Mayor, as the Local Chief Executive, and the Vice Mayor, as the Presiding Officer and a composite member of the sanggunian, and thus performing legislative functions. Accordingly, in a sanggunian with eight (8) regular members, two ex-officio members representing the Liga ng mga Barangay and the SK Federation and the Vice-Mayor as Presiding Officer, the total number of membership in that sanggunian, therefore, is eleven (II). Relative thereto, Section 53 of the Local Government Code provides that a majority of all the members of the sanggunian who have been elected and qualified shall constitute a quorum to transact official business. Hence, as provided for by law, quorum is the majority of all the members of that sanggunian. "Majority" has been defined by jurisprudence as that which is 50% plus 1 or that which is greater than half of the membership Of the body. We note, however, that using either formula will still give us the same result. For instance, if the membership of the sanggunian is II, II divided by 2 will give us 5.5. Hence, 5.5 plus 1 will give us 6.5. It is noted, however, that there can never be a fractional member of a sanggunian. Hence, the more appropriate thing to do is go down to the next lower whole number, which is 6. Corollary thereto, if we take the relationship of 6 vis-d-vis 5.5, 6 is definitely greater than 5.5, hence, 6 is greater than h of II. Under Section 49 of the same Code, if there are 6 members of your sanggunian present, but the Vice Mayor is absent, then the 6 members, which number already constitutes a quorum, shall elect from among themselves the Temporary Presiding Officer in the sanggunian. This applies to both regular and special sessions of the Sangguniang. In reply to your second and third queries, may we note that Section 54 of the Code provides: "SEC. 54. Approval of Ordinances.- (a) Every ordinance enacted by the xxx sangguniang bayan shall be presented to the xxx municipal mayor, as the case

-3- may be. If the local chief executive concerned approves the same, he shall affix his signature on each and every page thereof; otherwise, he shall veto it and return the same with his objections to the sanggunian, which may proceed to reconsider the same xxx." (underlining ours) For clarification, therefore, may we point out that when at the sanggunian level, a measure or ordinance has already been approved, the same is not yet called an approved ordinance but rather it is called an "enacted" ordinance only. Precisely, per Section 54 of the Code, what is to be submitted to the Local Chief Executive for his approval is the "enacted" ordinance of the sanggunian. Once the enacted ordinance is approved by the Mayor, it now becomes and called as "approved ordinance". Corollarily, the Local Government Code failed to provide a period within which for the sanggunian to transmit to the Local Chief Executive an enacted ordinance for his approval. The absence of a provision, however, should not defeat public trust as we can simply apply the period provided for under RA 6713, otherwise known as the "The Code of Conduct and Ethical Standards for Government Officials and Employees" wherein public officials are mandated to act on matters presented before them within fifteen (15) days from receipt thereof. Therefore, we are of the belief that the 15-day period provided for under RA 6713 can be analogously applied to determine the number of days within which for the sanggunian to transmit to the Local Chief Executive an enacted ordinance for his approval. May we note further that under Section 469 (c) (3) of the Local Government Code, it shall be the duty of the Secretary to the Sanggunian to forward to the Mayor for approval copies of ordinances enacted by the sanggunian and duly certified by the Presiding Officer. In this regard, the phrase "duly certified by the Presiding Officer" means that the Vice Mayor as Presiding Officer or any Temporary Presiding Officer for that matter, shall have certified that a session was indeed conducted whereupon the ordinance to be submitted was deliberated upon and duly enacted by the sanggunian concerned. At this juncture, it may be well to note that nowhere in the Local Government Code or other existing rules and regulations that members Of the sangguniang bayan are required to sign the enacted ordinance. Anyway, the Presiding Officer has already duly certified as to its enactment. Besides, the votes of the Sangguniang Bayan Members were already taken after the deliberation and properly reflected in the Minutes of that particular session where said proposed ordinance was deliberated upon and approved by the body. Hence, with respect to the sanggunian members who refuse to sign, there may be no liability since, in fact, the law does not require the signing, unless it is represented that they will Sign only in exchange of something. In such case, this demand for something may constitute a violation of RA 3019, otherwise known as the Anti-Graft and Corrupt Practices Act. If it is the Vice Mayor who will refuse to sign by reason alone that everybody present in that session had not yet signed, his refusal has no legal basis to stand. May it be reiterated that it is the duty of the Vice Mayor to duly certify an enacted ordinance. Accordingly, for these sanggunian members who demand something, and for the Vice Mayor who refuses to certify an enacted ordinance without any justifiable basis, there could be possible administrative or criminal case that could be filed against them, such as violation of RA 3019 (The Anti-Graft and Corrupt Practices Act) and other existing laws, as may be warranted by the evidence. In reply to your fourth query, regarding the declaration of calamity by the sangguniang bayan, you posed a hypothetical scenario that, for instance, only 5 out of the 9 regular members, one member happens to be on leave, signed the Resolution to make use of the calamity fund, and the 4 others, together with the Presiding Officer (Vice Mayor), refused to sign, what is your legal remedy?

-4- In reply thereto, your statement as to the 9 regular members is not so clear to us. Be that as it may, may we reiterate the membership of the sanggunian as stated above, that is, 8 regular members, 2 ex-officio members and 1 Presiding Officer. Hence, your sanggunian has a total membership of II. Where, however, one of the members is on leave, the ruling in the case of Avelino Y}. Cuenco (83 Phil. 17) becomes instructive. In said case, the Supreme Court held that: "the Supreme Court excluded a Member of the Senate in the determination of quorum for the reason that said Senator was in the United States and, therefore, outside the coercive jurisdiction of the Senate". Accordingly, applying by analogy the jurisprudence to the situation in the sanggunian where 1 member is on leave, the latter can, therefore, be considered as outside the coercive authority of the sanggunian. Hence, the quorum should be reckoned only from out of the IO members Of the sanggunian. Therefore, in a sanggunian of 10 members, the quorum is 6, which is the majority of 10. So, assuming that the remaining IO members (the on-leave member excluded) are all present in that particular session in order for the sanggunian to declare a state of calamity, a øositive vote of 6 members must be mustered since this number is the majority of those present. May we note that RA 8185 (An Act Amending Section 324 [d] of the Local Government Code) and its Implementing Rules and Regulations, did not provide for a specific voting requirement. It simply provided that the sanggunian, through a Resolution, shall declare a state of calamity. Hence, in the absence of an express provision requiring a different number of votes required to approve a particular measure, the rule is, it has to be approved by only a simple majority, meaning, majority vote of those present there being a quorum. In the meantime, the Implementing Rules and Regulations of RA 8185 allows the Mayor to incur cash advance of not more than 50% of the calamity fund provided, subsequently, the sangguniang bayan shall declare a state of calamity. On your last queries, as to whether or not there is a need for the Sangguniang Bayan to pass a Resolution declaring a state of calamity in the municipality should the province or the national government already declared a state of calamity, please be informed that we are talking here of two (2) kinds of calamity funds, which are: (I) the national calamity fund; and (2) the local calamity fund of the provinces, cities, municipalities and barangays, respectively. May we note that under the old Section 324 (d) of the Local Government Code, the local calamity fund can be utilized for unforeseen expenditures only when the President of the Republic declares a state of calamity. This Section 324 (d) of the Code, however, was amended by RA 8185, conferring to the local government units, through their sanggunians, the power to determine and declare a local state of calamity. This is precisely in recognition of the constitutional principle• of local autonomy. It is noted that despite the amendment of Section 324 (d) of the Code, the President can still declare a state of calamity but such declaration would be relevant only insofar as providing for the legal justification in disbursing the national calamity fund appropriated in the General Appropriations Act. The requirement of the law is very clear, that local calamity fund can only be released upon declaration of the sanggunian concerned of a state of calamity [Section 5 (a) (2), Implementing Rules and Regulations of RA 8185]. Accordingly, it does not follow that when the President of the Philippines declares an area to be under a State Of calamity, the local government units covered by such declaration can already disburse also their local calamity funds. The local government units concerned, through their sanggunians, have still to declare their own state of calamity to legally justify the disbursement of local calamity funds. With respect to the provincial declaration of state of calamity, may we note that in the Implementing Rules and Regulations of RA 8185, when the province declares

-5- a portion of its territory under a state of calamity, the municipalities covered or outside the declared area cannot as yet immediately utilize their own municipal calamity fund. They have to declare, through its sanggunian, their own state of calamity in order to justify the disbursement of their municipal calamity funds. However, when the province declares its entire territory to be under a state of calamity, the component municipalities of said province need not anymore declare its own state of calamity such that the provincial declaration of calamity can now be the legal basis for the municipality to disburse its municipal calamity fund. We hope we have enlightened you on the matter. Legal:43/La Director Leonilo B. Lariosa DILG Region IV-A Calderon Bldg., EDSA Diliman, Quezon City Director Rolando M.
